passages.passage_text: Researchers studied conditioned taste aversion in 40 adult laboratory rats. On the conditioning day, each rat drank a novel saccharin-flavored solution for 20 minutes. Rats were then randomly assigned (n = 10 per group) to receive an injection of lithium chloride, a drug that causes nausea, either 30 minutes, 6 hours, or 24 hours after drinking, or an injection of saline 30 minutes after drinking. Two days later, each rat was offered the saccharin solution again for 20 minutes, and the volume consumed was measured. Lithium chloride produced nausea lasting about 2 hours, and no rat received a second injection. Results are shown in Table 1. In a follow-up, rats from the 30-minute lithium group were offered saccharin for five consecutive daily tests with no further injections. Their mean intake rose steadily across the tests, reaching 11.9 mL on the fifth day. The investigators noted that rats rarely develop aversions to the sounds or lights present in the testing room, even when these accompany the nausea.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Saccharin intake at test (mL, mean with SD in parentheses)**

| Group (n = 10 each) | Intake |
|---|---|
| Saline, 30 min after drinking | 14.2 (2.1) |
| Lithium, 30 min after drinking | 3.1 (1.8) |
| Lithium, 6 h after drinking | 5.4 (2.4) |
| Lithium, 24 h after drinking | 12.8 (2.6) |

questions.stem: After conditioning, the saccharin solution in the lithium groups is best described as a:

options.A: unconditioned stimulus that naturally elicits nausea.
options.B: conditioned response that reflects the rats' learned avoidance.
options.C: conditioned stimulus that now elicits an aversive response.
options.D: negative reinforcer that increases the drinking of saccharin.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Saccharin began as a neutral taste and, through pairing with nausea, acquired the ability to elicit avoidance, which defines a conditioned stimulus. Why the others are wrong: A) The nausea-inducing drug is the unconditioned stimulus; saccharin did not cause illness on its own. B) The avoidance is the response; saccharin is the stimulus that triggers it. D) Intake fell, and a stimulus that is removed to strengthen a behavior is not what was manipulated here.
questions.trap: Confusing the learned stimulus (CS) with the learned response (CR), or calling the drug the CS because it was the 'treatment.'

questions.stem: Intake in the 6-hour lithium group (5.4 mL) was far below that of the saline group (14.2 mL). This result is notable because it shows that:

options.A: conditioning occurred only because the saccharin and the lithium injection were presented at the same moment.
options.B: the rats had habituated to the saccharin solution during conditioning.
options.C: learning of a flavor-illness association can form despite a delay of hours between the CS and US.
options.D: the lithium injection acted as a conditioned stimulus for the saccharin taste.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Most classical conditioning requires the CS and US to be close in time, but taste-illness learning is biologically prepared and tolerates long delays. Why the others are wrong: A) The injection came 6 hours after drinking, so the two stimuli were not simultaneous. B) Habituation would not lower intake relative to the saline control, which drank the same solution. D) Lithium is the unconditioned stimulus; the saccharin taste is the one that gained meaning.
questions.trap: Assuming that all classical conditioning needs a half-second-to-seconds interval and so reading the 6-hour effect as a methodological flaw.

questions.stem: The gradual rise in saccharin intake to 11.9 mL across five tests without further injections illustrates:

options.A: spontaneous recovery, because the aversion reappeared after a rest period.
options.B: extinction, because the CS was repeatedly presented without the US.
options.C: stimulus generalization, because the rats drank similar flavors.
options.D: sensitization, because exposure heightened the rats' responses.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Repeated presentation of the CS alone weakens the conditioned response, so intake gradually returns toward baseline. Why the others are wrong: A) Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a pause; here the aversion was weakening, not returning. C) Generalization concerns responses to stimuli resembling the CS, which were not tested. D) Sensitization would increase responsiveness to stimuli and would not produce increased drinking.
questions.trap: Reading any change in a conditioned response over time as spontaneous recovery rather than recognizing the decline as extinction.

questions.stem: The saline-injected group was included primarily to:

options.A: rule out that handling or injection alone reduced saccharin intake.
options.B: measure how much saccharin intake rises after repeated extinction trials without lithium.
options.C: increase the sample size available for the comparison with the 24-hour delay group.
options.D: confirm that lithium chloride acts as an unconditioned stimulus that produces nausea.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Because that group went through the same procedure except for the drug, differences in intake can be attributed to pairing with lithium. Why the others are wrong: B) Extinction was assessed in the lithium group, not the saline group. C) The saline group was a separate comparison and did not add to the 24-hour group. D) That lithium causes nausea is known from prior work and is not tested by a saline group.
questions.trap: Thinking a control group exists to enlarge the sample or to test the drug itself instead of isolating the manipulated variable.

questions.stem: Relative to the saline group, the percentage reduction in saccharin intake in the 30-minute lithium group was closest to:
questions.explanation: Correct: B) (14.2 - 3.1) / 14.2 = 11.1 / 14.2, or about 78%. Why the others are wrong: A) This is 3.1 / 14.2, the intake as a fraction of control rather than the reduction. C) This is the reduction for the 6-hour group, (14.2 - 5.4) / 14.2. D) This would require intake of about 1.6 mL; it is not supported by the table.
questions.trap: Reporting the remaining intake (22%) as the reduction instead of subtracting it from 100%.

passages.passage_text: Pure-tone audiometry was used to measure hearing thresholds in three groups of adults with no history of ear disease or noisy occupations: young (ages 20 to 29), middle-aged (50 to 59), and older (70 to 79), with 40 participants per group. Each participant listened through headphones to tones at four frequencies, and the threshold was defined as the lowest intensity, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), detected on 50% of presentations. Higher values therefore indicate poorer hearing. Mean thresholds are shown in Figure 1. To determine the site of the loss, thresholds at 4000 Hz were also measured by bone conduction, in which a vibrator on the skull bypasses the outer and middle ear. These results are shown in Table 1 for the older group and for a comparison group of 10 adults with fluid behind the eardrum. Postmortem examination of cochleae from a separate set of older donors showed that loss of hair cells was greatest near the cochlear base and minimal near the apex.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Mean thresholds at 4000 Hz (dB HL)**

| Group | Air conduction | Bone conduction |
|---|---|---|
| Older adults (n = 40) | 52 | 49 |
| Middle-ear fluid (n = 10) | 40 | 5 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean hearing threshold by frequency and age group

questions.stem: Which structural change best accounts for the greater high-frequency loss in older adults?

options.A: Loss of hair cells near the apex of the cochlea, where the basilar membrane is wide and floppy
options.B: Stiffening of the tympanic membrane and ossicles, which impairs transmission of sound to the cochlea
options.C: Degeneration of the vestibular hair cells in the semicircular canals that sense head rotation
options.D: Loss of hair cells along the stiff basilar membrane near the cochlear base

questions.explanation: Correct: D) High frequencies maximally displace the basilar membrane near the base, so hair-cell loss there impairs high-pitched hearing first. Why the others are wrong: A) The apex encodes low frequencies, and the donor cochleae showed minimal apical loss. B) Conductive changes would raise bone-conduction thresholds less than air thresholds, which was not the pattern in the older group. C) The vestibular system contributes to balance, not to detecting tones.
questions.trap: Choosing the apex because 'older' suggests low sounds, forgetting that high frequencies are coded at the base.

questions.stem: The elevation in threshold of older adults relative to young adults at 8000 Hz is about how many times the elevation at 1000 Hz?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) At 8000 Hz the elevation is 70 - 12 = 58 dB; at 1000 Hz it is 22 - 5 = 17 dB; 58 / 17 is about 3.4. Why the others are wrong: A) 1.5 does not match any pair of readings in Figure 1 and understates the 8000 Hz elevation relative to 1000 Hz. C) Neither pair of read values gives this ratio; it would underestimate the difference at 8000 Hz. D) This is far too large; the older group's thresholds are 70 versus 22 dB, a ratio of about 3.2 even before subtracting baselines.
questions.trap: Dividing raw thresholds (70/22) instead of first subtracting each frequency's young-adult baseline.

questions.stem: The older group's air-conduction (52 dB) and bone-conduction (49 dB) thresholds at 4000 Hz indicate that their loss is mainly:

options.A: sensorineural, because bypassing the middle ear does not help.
options.B: conductive, because the air-conduction threshold is elevated above normal.
options.C: conductive, because damage to the ossicles reduces sound transmission.
options.D: cortical, because the sound reaches the inner ear normally.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) If the problem were in the outer or middle ear, bone conduction would be much better than air conduction, as in the middle-ear fluid group (5 versus 40 dB). Why the others are wrong: B) Elevated air thresholds occur in both types; the air-bone gap distinguishes them, and the gap here is only 3 dB. C) Ossicle damage would produce a large air-bone gap, which is absent. D) The elevated bone-conduction threshold points to the cochlea or auditory nerve, and the histology supports a cochlear cause.
questions.trap: Seeing high air-conduction thresholds and concluding 'conductive' without comparing air and bone values.

questions.stem: The threshold values measured in this study correspond to the psychophysical concept of:

options.A: difference threshold, the smallest detectable change between two stimuli of different intensity.
options.B: sensory adaptation, the reduced responsiveness of receptors to constant stimulation.
options.C: signal detection, the separation of sensitivity from response bias in a decision.
options.D: absolute threshold, the minimum intensity detected 50% of the time.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The study defined threshold as the lowest intensity detected on half of presentations, which is the standard definition of absolute threshold. Why the others are wrong: A) Difference thresholds involve comparing two stimuli, not detecting a single tone. B) Adaptation concerns declining responses during sustained stimulation and was not measured. C) No catch trials or bias measures were described.
questions.trap: Mixing absolute threshold with the just-noticeable difference because both are called 'thresholds.'

questions.stem: For an older adult whose profound loss is due to destruction of cochlear hair cells, which intervention directly addresses the deficit?

options.A: A cochlear implant that stimulates the auditory nerve
options.B: Tympanostomy tubes inserted to drain fluid from the middle ear
options.C: An ossicular prosthesis to replace the damaged middle-ear bones
options.D: Surgical removal of impacted earwax from the ear canal

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The implant bypasses damaged hair cells and delivers electrical signals to auditory nerve fibers. Why the others are wrong: B) Tubes treat middle-ear fluid, a conductive problem. C) This would address conductive loss, which this group did not have. D) Earwax blockage affects sound transmission to the eardrum, not hair-cell function.
questions.trap: Matching any ear procedure to 'hearing loss' without checking whether the site is conductive or sensorineural.

passages.passage_text: Fourteen healthy adults slept for two consecutive nights in a sleep laboratory while polysomnography recorded EEG, eye movements, and chin muscle tone. The first night was used for adaptation, and data were taken from the second night. Recordings were scored in 30-second epochs as wakefulness, stage N1, N2, or N3 (non-REM sleep), or REM sleep. During each stage, an experimenter played a 1-second tone that began at 40 dB and rose in 5-dB steps every 30 seconds until the participant awoke; the loudness at awakening was the arousal threshold. Mean values are shown in Table 1. During N2 sleep, participants also heard the same 50-dB tone every 10 seconds. The amplitude of the EEG response to the tone declined over the first several minutes of repetition, but a recording of the sleeper's own name, played afterward, produced a large response. Total sleep time averaged 420 minutes. Participants avoided caffeine and alcohol on study days, and the scorers did not know when the tones were played.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Sleep stages (second night, n = 14)**

| Stage | Dominant EEG pattern | Mean time (min) | Mean arousal threshold (dB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 | Theta waves (4-7 Hz) | 21 | 52 |
| N2 | Theta waves with sleep spindles and K-complexes | 210 | 62 |
| N3 | High-amplitude delta waves (below 4 Hz) | 84 | 78 |
| REM | Low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity | 105 | 66 |

questions.stem: A participant is awakened during the stage marked by low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG activity, rapid eye movements, and loss of chin muscle tone. The participant is most likely to report:

options.A: a vivid, story-like dream.
options.B: a brief sensation of falling, with no organized imagery.
options.C: no mental activity, but a short period of sleepwalking.
options.D: a clear memory of the tones played during the night.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) REM sleep combines wake-like cortical activity with muscle atonia, and awakenings from it yield vivid, narrative dreams most often. Why the others are wrong: B) Hypnic jerks and falling sensations occur at sleep onset in N1, which shows theta waves and slow rolling eye movements. C) Sleepwalking arises from deep N3 sleep, when muscle tone is preserved, not from REM, when voluntary muscles are paralyzed. D) Sleeping people do not form lasting memories of ordinary external stimuli, and this stage has no special link to remembering tones.
questions.trap: Matching low-amplitude, mixed EEG to light non-REM sleep because the waves are small, rather than recognizing the wake-like pattern of REM.

questions.stem: What percentage of total sleep time was spent in stage N3?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) 84 min / 420 min = 0.20, or 20%. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the share for N1 (21/420), the shortest stage. B) This is the share for REM sleep (105/420), not N3. D) This is N3 divided by N2 (84/210), which uses the wrong denominator instead of total sleep time.
questions.trap: Dividing by the time in another stage instead of by the total sleep time.

questions.stem: The declining EEG response to the repeated 50-dB tone, together with the large response to the sleeper's own name, is best described as:

options.A: sensitization to the tone, in which repeated exposure produces a progressively stronger response to it and to similar stimuli.
options.B: habituation to the repeated tone, with the personally meaningful name still capturing attention.
options.C: extinction of a conditioned response, in which a learned association fades when the tone is presented repeatedly without its usual consequence.
options.D: spontaneous recovery of a learned response, in which a response reappears after a rest period, here when the name replaced the tone.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Repeated exposure to a harmless stimulus reduces responding, and a novel, meaningful stimulus is not habituated to, so the name evokes a large response. Why the others are wrong: A) Sensitization would raise the response with repetition; the data show a decline. C) Extinction requires an earlier learned association that stops being reinforced; no association was trained here. D) Spontaneous recovery refers to a conditioned response reappearing after a rest period, which does not describe a new stimulus (the name) evoking a response.
questions.trap: Calling any decline in responding extinction, even though extinction requires an earlier learned association.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers use data from the second night rather than the first?

options.A: Sleep stages cannot be scored reliably until a participant has been recorded for at least two nights.
options.B: Total sleep time always doubles on the second night, so its data give a larger sample of epochs.
options.C: Participants on the first night would have heard tones that altered the arousal thresholds measured later.
options.D: An unfamiliar room and equipment can disturb first-night sleep, which would distort stage durations.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) A first-night effect (lighter, more fragmented sleep in an unfamiliar setting) is a known confound, and an adaptation night reduces it. Why the others are wrong: A) Scoring in 30-second epochs is possible from any recording; no minimum number of nights is needed. B) Sleep duration does not systematically double; the adaptation night addresses sleep quality, not sample size. C) The tones were played on the data night, not before it; the adaptation night addressed environment effects.
questions.trap: Treating the adaptation night as a way to collect more data instead of a control for an unfamiliar environment.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The loudest tone was needed to awaken sleepers from the delta-wave stage, indicating the deepest sleep.
options.B: Arousal threshold fell steadily from N1 through REM as the night went on, so sleep became lighter with each successive stage.
options.C: REM sleep is the deepest stage because its EEG pattern differs most from that of wakefulness.
options.D: N2 is the stage from which participants were hardest to awaken, because it accounted for the longest share of the night.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) N3 had the highest mean threshold (78 dB) and slow, high-amplitude delta waves, consistent with deep slow-wave sleep. Why the others are wrong: B) Thresholds rose from N1 (52) to N3 (78) before falling to 66 in REM; they did not fall steadily, and the table does not track time across the night. C) REM thresholds (66 dB) are lower than N3 (78 dB), and its wake-like EEG suggests a more active brain, not a deeper sleep by this measure. D) Duration does not determine arousal difficulty; N2 had a threshold of 62 dB, below both N3 (78) and REM (66).
questions.trap: Equating the stage with the longest duration with the deepest sleep, instead of using the arousal-threshold column.

passages.passage_text: A university research team surveyed 1,200 undergraduates about their social media use. Students reported their average daily hours on social platforms and completed a 20-item loneliness scale (score range 20 to 80; higher scores indicate greater loneliness) and a sleep diary. Participants were recruited through an introductory psychology course at one university and received course credit. Pearson correlations are shown in Table 1. Six months later, 900 of the students completed the same measures again, and the researchers computed cross-lagged correlations between the two time points (Table 2). Figure 1 shows mean loneliness scores for students grouped by reported daily use at the first survey. The authors cautioned against causal conclusions but proposed that heavy use might displace time spent in face-to-face contact and invite unfavorable comparisons with peers. They also noted that participants may have misjudged their own hours of use and that students who completed the second survey were somewhat less lonely at baseline than those who did not.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Correlations at the first survey (n = 1,200)**

| Variables | r | p |
|---|---|---|
| Daily use and loneliness | +0.24 | < 0.001 |
| Daily use and hours of sleep | -0.18 | < 0.001 |
| Hours of sleep and loneliness | -0.31 | < 0.001 |

**Table 2. Cross-lagged correlations (n = 900)**

| Path | r | p |
|---|---|---|
| Use at survey 1 and loneliness at survey 2 | +0.09 | 0.03 |
| Loneliness at survey 1 and use at survey 2 | +0.17 | < 0.001 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean loneliness score by daily social media use
graph.x_label: Reported daily use, midpoint of group (hours)

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of the variance in loneliness is shared with daily use at the first survey?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.24 x 0.24 = 0.058, or about 6%. Why the others are wrong: A) This treats r itself as the proportion of variance shared. C) Doubling r would not give the shared variance. D) Doubling the correlation again mistakes r for a percentage.
questions.trap: Reading r = 0.24 as 24% of variance explained instead of squaring it.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the Table 1 data?

options.A: Heavy use causes loneliness, because the correlation between the two is statistically significant at p < 0.001.
options.B: Use and loneliness are associated, but a third variable such as poor sleep could contribute to both.
options.C: Use and loneliness are unrelated, because the correlation coefficient is below 0.30 in magnitude.
options.D: Loneliness reduces sleep, which in turn causes heavier use, as shown by the signs of the correlations.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The data are correlational, and sleep is related to both use and loneliness, so it is a plausible confounder. Why the others are wrong: A) Significance shows that the association is unlikely due to chance, not that one variable causes the other. C) An r of 0.24 with n = 1,200 is a significant, if modest, association. D) Correlation signs cannot establish a causal chain.
questions.trap: Equating statistical significance with demonstration of causation.

questions.stem: Compared with the use-to-loneliness path, the loneliness-to-use path in Table 2 suggests that:

options.A: social media use clearly causes later loneliness, because use was measured at the first time point.
options.B: neither path is statistically significant at the conventional 0.05 level.
options.C: earlier loneliness predicted later use somewhat more strongly than the reverse.
options.D: the two variables had no relationship at either of the two time points.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The correlation from loneliness to later use (+0.17) exceeds the correlation in the other direction (+0.09), though neither proves causation. Why the others are wrong: A) Temporal order is necessary but not sufficient for causal inference, and the larger path runs the other way. B) Both p-values are below 0.05. D) All correlations in both tables are significant.
questions.trap: Assuming the variable measured first must be the cause, despite the larger cross-lagged path going the other way.

questions.stem: Which feature of the sampling most limits generalization of these findings to all adults?

options.A: The sample included more than 1,000 students, which exceeds many comparable surveys.
options.B: Loneliness was measured with a 20-item scale instead of a single question.
options.C: Some students were lost between the first and second surveys, six months apart.
options.D: Participants were volunteers from one university's introductory course.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) A convenience sample of young students at one school may differ in age, education, and social context from the broader population. Why the others are wrong: A) Large samples improve precision and do not limit generalization by themselves. B) Scale length relates to reliability, not to which population was sampled. C) Attrition threatens internal validity of the longitudinal analysis, rather than generalization to adults as a whole.
questions.trap: Confusing a large sample size with a representative sample.

questions.stem: Which psychological process best fits the authors' proposal about 'unfavorable comparisons with peers'?

options.A: The looking-glass self, in which a person is shaped by the unconscious reactions of strangers.
options.B: The fundamental attribution error, in which dispositions are overemphasized in explaining others' behavior.
options.C: Cognitive dissonance, in which conflicting attitudes produce discomfort.
options.D: Social comparison, in which people evaluate their own abilities and status against those of others.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) According to social comparison theory, upward comparisons with peers who appear more successful or more connected can lower self-evaluation. Why the others are wrong: A) The looking-glass self concerns imagined judgments of others, not comparisons of self to peers. B) This is about explaining others' behavior. C) Dissonance concerns inconsistency between beliefs or between beliefs and behavior.
questions.trap: Choosing the looking-glass self because it also involves other people, without noting the process is comparison to peers.

passages.passage_text: In a study of short-term retention, 120 adults were shown a list of 20 unrelated common nouns, one word every 2 seconds at the center of a computer screen. Participants were tested individually in a quiet room and were told in advance that they would be asked to recall the list. They were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (n = 60 each). In the immediate condition, participants wrote down as many words as they could remember, in any order, as soon as the list ended. In the delay condition, participants first counted backward by threes from a three-digit number for 30 seconds and then began writing. For each condition, researchers computed the percentage of participants who correctly recalled the word at each serial position. Figure 1 shows results for selected positions. Mean total recall was 11.4 words in the immediate condition and 8.1 words in the delay condition.

graph.title: Figure 1. Percentage recalling the word at each serial position

questions.stem: The loss of the advantage for the final list items in the delay condition is best explained by:

options.A: the final items having been poorly encoded into long-term memory because the list was long and fast.
options.B: the final items having been held in short-term memory and then lost during counting.
options.C: retroactive facilitation from the counting task strengthening the earlier items in the list.
options.D: a decline in implicit procedural memory caused by the interruption after the list ended.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Late items are recalled from working memory in the immediate condition; counting prevents rehearsal and displaces them, so the recency advantage disappears. Why the others are wrong: A) Early and middle items were not affected by the delay, which does not support a general encoding failure. C) Early-item recall was nearly unchanged, and a distraction task would not strengthen any item. D) Procedural memory concerns skills, not recall of words.
questions.trap: Attributing the recency loss to long-term forgetting, when the surviving primacy items show long-term storage was intact.

questions.stem: The high recall of the first few words in both conditions most likely reflects:

options.A: their storage in the sensory register, which holds the first items for several seconds.
options.B: greater rehearsal of early items, promoting their transfer to long-term memory.
options.C: their encoding as a single chunk of seven items in working memory.
options.D: the serial position curve being created by the interference from the counting task.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Early items receive more rehearsal before the list fills working memory, so they are stored more durably and are unaffected by the delay. Why the others are wrong: A) Sensory memory lasts only a second or two and could not survive the counting task. C) Chunking is not suggested by a list of unrelated words. D) Primacy was present in the immediate condition, which had no counting task.
questions.trap: Assigning the primacy effect to short-term storage rather than to long-term transfer.

questions.stem: At serial position 20, the percentage-point difference between the immediate and delay conditions is:
questions.explanation: Correct: A) 88% - 34% = 54 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the delay condition's value alone. C) This arises from misreading one of the values at position 20 by 10. D) Misreading either value by 10 would give 64; neither is shown by the graph.
questions.trap: Reporting one condition's value instead of subtracting the two.

questions.stem: Why did participants in the delay condition count backward rather than simply wait for 30 seconds?

options.A: To increase the number of words stored in long-term memory.
options.B: To make the delay and immediate conditions equal in total time.
options.C: To measure working-memory capacity through the counting performance.
options.D: To prevent rehearsal of the last items during the delay.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Without a distractor, participants could keep rehearsing recent words, preserving the recency effect and confounding the effect of time with that of rehearsal. Why the others are wrong: A) Counting would not enhance storage. B) The delay condition lasted 30 seconds longer by design. C) Counting accuracy was not analyzed.
questions.trap: Assuming that a filler task is intended to improve learning rather than block rehearsal.

passages.passage_text: In a variant of an obedience experiment, 120 adults were randomly assigned to four conditions (n = 30 each). Each participant, cast as a "teacher," was told to deliver electric shocks of rising intensity, up to 450 V, to a "learner" (a confederate who received no shocks) for each wrong answer on a word-pair test. If the teacher hesitated, an experimenter gave a series of standard verbal prods, such as "The experiment requires that you continue." In the first condition, the experimenter wore a lab coat and sat in the room. In the second, he gave the same instructions by telephone from another room. In the third, he sat in the room but wore ordinary clothes. In the fourth, a second "teacher" (a confederate) refused to continue partway through the session. All participants were debriefed and told that no shocks were delivered. The proportion who delivered the maximum shock is shown in Table 1. Participants had no prior coursework in psychology, and the same two experimenters ran all sessions using a written script.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Obedience by condition (n = 30 per condition)**

| Condition | Delivered 450 V, n | Delivered 450 V, % |
|---|---|---|
| Lab coat, experimenter in room | 20 | 67% |
| Experimenter instructing by telephone | 7 | 23% |
| Ordinary clothes, experimenter in room | 14 | 47% |
| Peer teacher refuses to continue | 3 | 10% |

questions.stem: The lower rate of full obedience in the telephone condition than in the in-room, lab coat condition best supports which conclusion?

options.A: Obedience depends mainly on the learner's apparent suffering, which was the same in both conditions.
options.B: Obedience reflects the authority figure's attire, which the telephone condition removed entirely.
options.C: Obedience is greater when the authority figure is physically close and able to monitor compliance.
options.D: Obedience reflects the group size, which the telephone condition reduced from two people to one.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Proximity and surveillance of the authority increase compliance, so remote instruction produced fewer maximum shocks (23% vs. 67%). Why the others are wrong: A) The learner's behavior was not varied across these conditions, so it cannot account for the difference between them. B) Attire was varied only in the third condition; a telephone instruction differs from the in-room condition mainly in how present and watchful the authority is, not in attire alone. D) Group size was not manipulated between these two conditions; in each, one participant faced one experimenter.
questions.trap: Attributing a difference to a variable (such as attire or suffering) that was not manipulated between the two conditions compared.

questions.stem: The sharp drop in obedience when a peer teacher refused to continue is best explained by:

options.A: the presence of a dissenting peer, which legitimizes disobedience and reduces pressure to comply.
options.B: social facilitation, in which the presence of an audience or co-actors improves performance on simple or well-learned tasks.
options.C: deindividuation, in which immersion in a group lowers self-awareness and personal accountability for harmful acts.
options.D: groupthink, in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent and overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives to preserve unanimity.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A model of defiance shows that refusal is possible and weakens the authority's influence, as in research on resistance to authority. Why the others are wrong: B) Social facilitation concerns performance effects of an audience, not a decision to continue or refuse an order. C) Deindividuation would increase harmful compliance in a group; here the peer's refusal reduced it. D) Groupthink describes cohesive groups suppressing dissent; the dissenting peer here was followed rather than suppressed.
questions.trap: Choosing a familiar group-behavior term (groupthink, deindividuation) without checking whether its predicted direction matches the result.

questions.stem: Approximately how many times as large was the proportion delivering 450 V in the lab coat, in-room condition as in the telephone condition?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) 20 / 7 = 2.86, or about 2.9 times. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the inverse ratio (7/20), which compares the telephone condition to the in-room condition. B) This is the difference in the number of participants (20 - 7), not a ratio. C) This is the difference between the percentages (66.7 - 23.3 = 43.3), which is in percentage points, not a ratio.
questions.trap: Subtracting two values when the question asks for a ratio, or inverting the ratio.

questions.stem: Which design feature most directly allows a comparison of the lab coat and ordinary clothes conditions to isolate the effect of attire?

options.A: Debriefing of all participants, which equalized their knowledge of the study afterward.
options.B: Random assignment, with location, prods, and learner responses held constant across the two conditions.
options.C: Use of a confederate as the learner, which ensured that no shocks were actually delivered.
options.D: The inclusion of 30 participants per condition, which makes any difference statistically significant.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Only attire differed between the two conditions, and random assignment spread participant characteristics evenly. Why the others are wrong: A) Debriefing occurs after the data are collected and cannot affect behavior during the experiment. C) Using a confederate protects participants' welfare and standardizes the learner's responses but does not isolate attire. D) A sample of 30 per group does not guarantee statistical significance, and sample size does not isolate a variable.
questions.trap: Confusing ethical or procedural safeguards with features that control confounding variables.

passages.passage_text: Pigeons were trained to peck a key for food. Thirty-two pigeons, each reduced to 85% of free-feeding body weight, were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 8 each) that differed only in the reinforcement schedule. Fixed-ratio 10 (FR-10): food after every 10th peck. Variable-ratio 10 (VR-10): food after an unpredictable number of pecks that averaged 10. Fixed-interval 30 s (FI-30): food for the first peck after 30 seconds had elapsed since the last food. Variable-interval 30 s (VI-30): food for the first peck after an unpredictable interval averaging 30 seconds. After 20 daily sessions, mean peck rate was recorded. Food was then withheld entirely, and the experimenters counted total pecks until 5 minutes passed with no peck. Results are shown in Table 1. Responding on the FI-30 schedule showed a pause after each food delivery, followed by an increasing rate as the end of the interval approached. Sessions lasted 40 minutes, and the chamber, key, and food hopper were identical for every group.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Pecking by schedule (n = 8 per group)**

| Schedule | Mean pecks per minute | Mean total pecks after food was withheld |
|---|---|---|
| FR-10 | 62 | 95 |
| VR-10 | 78 | 410 |
| FI-30 | 24 | 120 |
| VI-30 | 36 | 260 |

questions.stem: Gambling on a slot machine, which pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, most resembles which schedule?

options.A: Variable-ratio
options.B: Fixed-ratio
options.C: Variable-interval
options.D: Fixed-interval

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Payoff depends on the number of responses, which varies unpredictably; this is variable-ratio and it sustains high, steady rates. Why the others are wrong: B) Fixed-ratio pays after a set number of responses, which a slot machine does not do. C) Variable-interval depends on elapsed time, not on the number of plays, so playing faster would not bring a payout sooner. D) Fixed-interval depends on a predictable amount of elapsed time, not on the number of plays.
questions.trap: Choosing fixed-ratio because payouts are tied to responses, overlooking the unpredictability of the required number.

questions.stem: The much lower peck rate on FI-30 than on the ratio schedules is best explained by the fact that on an interval schedule:

options.A: food is delivered after a fixed number of pecks, which lets the bird rest once it has completed that required number.
options.B: the unpredictability of food delivery makes each peck equally likely to be reinforced.
options.C: extra pecks before the interval ends do not bring food sooner, so rate is not tied to number of pecks.
options.D: punishment is delivered for pecks made before the interval has elapsed, which suppresses responding early in the interval.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Reinforcement depends on time passing, so fast pecking does not increase food; the bird pecks little early in the interval. Why the others are wrong: A) A set number of pecks defines a fixed-ratio schedule, not a fixed-interval one. B) Fixed-interval schedules are predictable in timing, and the pecks made early in the interval are never reinforced. D) No punisher was used; early pecks are simply not reinforced, which is extinction-like, not punishment.
questions.trap: Assuming that all intermittent schedules produce similarly high response rates.

questions.stem: By approximately what percent did the mean peck rate on VR-10 exceed that on FR-10?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) The percent excess is (78 - 62) / 62 = 0.258, or about 26%. Why the others are wrong: A) The difference was divided by the larger rate (16/78 = 20.5%); the comparison group's rate should be the base. B) 16 is the raw difference in pecks per minute, not a percent of the FR-10 rate. D) This is the ratio 78/62 expressed as a percent (about 126%), which is the rate itself as a percent of FR-10 rather than the excess.
questions.trap: Dividing by the wrong baseline or reporting the raw difference as a percent.

questions.stem: Which result in Table 1 is best explained by the unpredictability of reinforcement on the variable schedules?

options.A: Fewer total pecks after food was withheld, because variable schedules weaken the link between pecking and food.
options.B: Greater persistence of pecking after food was withheld, because the absence of food is harder to detect.
options.C: A faster peck rate on VI-30 than on FR-10 during training, because interval schedules deliver food more often.
options.D: A pause after each food delivery, because the bird knew when the next food would be available.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Birds on variable schedules were used to long, irregular runs without food, so extinction does not stand out; they pecked 410 and 260 times, more than their fixed counterparts. Why the others are wrong: A) The table shows the opposite: variable groups pecked more after food was withheld (410 vs. 95; 260 vs. 120). C) VI-30 birds pecked 36 times per minute, slower than FR-10 birds at 62, so this result does not occur. D) The post-reinforcement pause is described for the fixed-interval schedule, where timing is predictable.
questions.trap: Expecting weaker responding from the less predictable schedule, which reverses the partial-reinforcement extinction effect.

passages.passage_text: Researchers tested whether intergroup contact reduces prejudice. Two hundred forty adolescents from two ethnic groups that had little prior contact were randomly assigned (n = 80 per condition) to a four-week program. In the cooperative contact condition, mixed-group teams of equal status worked toward a shared goal that no single group could reach alone, with support from program leaders. In the unstructured contact condition, adolescents shared a facility and meals but chose their own activities, and teams were not formed. In the no-contact condition, adolescents stayed in their own groups. Warmth toward the out-group was measured at baseline, at 4 weeks, and at 24 weeks, on a 0 to 100 thermometer (higher scores indicate warmer feelings). Results are summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1. The research assistants who collected the ratings did not know the condition assignments. Participants completed the ratings privately, and none left the program before the final assessment.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Mean out-group warmth (0 to 100)**

| Condition (n = 80 each) | Baseline | 4 weeks | 24 weeks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cooperative contact | 42 | 61 | 57 |
| Unstructured contact | 43 | 44 | 39 |
| No contact | 42 | 43 | 42 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean out-group warmth over time

questions.stem: Which feature of the cooperative contact condition is most consistent with the conditions that the contact hypothesis says are needed to reduce prejudice?

options.A: Equal-status teams pursuing a common goal with institutional support.
options.B: Frequent, casual exposure to out-group members in shared settings.
options.C: Random assignment of participants to a program instead of self-selection.
options.D: Measurement of attitudes at several time points after the program began.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Equal status, cooperation toward shared goals, and authority support are the classic conditions for contact to improve intergroup attitudes. Why the others are wrong: B) Mere exposure was present in the unstructured condition, where warmth did not rise, so it is not sufficient. C) Random assignment strengthens the design but is not a feature of the contact conditions that the theory describes. D) Repeated measurement is a design feature and does not itself change attitudes.
questions.trap: Assuming that simply being together reduces prejudice, even though the unstructured group shows little change.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely allow the unstructured contact condition to produce attitude gains similar to the cooperative condition?

options.A: Increasing the number of meals that adolescents from both groups share in the facility.
options.B: Adding a competition between the two ethnic groups to increase the salience of group identity.
options.C: Assigning mixed-group teams a goal that requires the efforts of members from both groups.
options.D: Reminding adolescents of their ethnic group membership before each activity.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Superordinate goals that require cooperation, as in Sherif's studies, convert two groups into one team and reduce bias. Why the others are wrong: A) More shared meals add exposure only; the unstructured group already had meals and shows no gain. B) Competition between groups increases hostility, as in Sherif's realistic conflict findings. D) Emphasizing category membership strengthens in-group versus out-group distinctions rather than reducing them.
questions.trap: Choosing more exposure, which fails to separate cooperation from simple contact.

questions.stem: In the cooperative contact condition, by approximately what percent did mean warmth decline from week 4 to week 24?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) (61 - 57) / 61 = 0.066, or about 7%. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the raw decline in points (4), not the percent. B) This divides the 4-point decline by the 19-point gain (4/19), which gives the share of the gain lost rather than the percent decline from week 4. C) This is the net gain from baseline relative to baseline (15/42), not the decline from week 4.
questions.trap: Dividing by the wrong reference value.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of including the no-contact condition?

options.A: To ensure that every adolescent receives the same amount of out-group exposure.
options.B: To show whether warmth changes with time and repeated testing even when no contact occurs.
options.C: To show that unstructured contact is more effective than cooperative contact.
options.D: To eliminate the need for random assignment to the other two conditions.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A control group that receives no contact reveals changes due to time, repeated measurement, or outside events, so program effects can be separated. Why the others are wrong: A) The no-contact group received no exposure, so the condition does not equalize exposure. C) The data show the opposite: cooperative contact produced the largest gain. D) Random assignment is needed for every group and cannot be replaced by a control group.
questions.trap: Treating a control group as something that substitutes for random assignment.

passages.passage_text: To study the development of conservation, researchers tested 180 children, 30 at each age from 4 to 9 years. In the number task, each child first agreed that two rows of six coins were equal, then watched as one row was spread out; the child was asked whether the rows still held the same number. In the liquid task, a child agreed that two identical glasses held equal amounts of juice, and then the juice from one glass was poured into a tall, thin glass; the child was asked whether the amounts were still equal. A child passed a task only by answering that the quantities were equal and giving a reason. Each child was tested once. Pass counts are shown in Table 1, and the percent passing is plotted in Figure 1. Testers followed a fixed script and scored the children's reasons using written criteria; any child who did not understand the instructions was retested on another day.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Children passing each task (n = 30 per age)**

| Age (years) | Number task, n passing | Liquid task, n passing |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 3 | 1 |
| 5 | 6 | 2 |
| 6 | 13 | 7 |
| 7 | 22 | 16 |
| 8 | 27 | 24 |
| 9 | 29 | 28 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Percent of children passing by age

questions.stem: How many more 6-year-olds passed the number task than passed the liquid task?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) 13 - 7 = 6 children. Why the others are wrong: B) 13 is the number passing the number task alone, not the difference. C) 20% is the difference in percentages (43% - 23%), which is in percentage points, not a count of children. D) 7 is the number passing the liquid task, not the difference between tasks.
questions.trap: Reporting one of the two table values or a percentage-point gap instead of the difference in counts.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old says the tall, thin glass holds more juice because it looks "taller." According to Piaget, this response most directly reflects:

options.A: egocentrism, an inability to take another person's perspective, typical of the sensorimotor stage (birth to age 2).
options.B: lack of object permanence, typical of the formal operational stage, which arises in adolescence.
options.C: centration on one dimension, typical of the preoperational stage.
options.D: reversible logic that applies only to abstract hypotheses, typical of the concrete operational stage.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Preoperational children center on one salient feature (height) and cannot yet coordinate height with width, so they fail to conserve. Why the others are wrong: A) Egocentrism is a preoperational feature, but it concerns perspective-taking, and the sensorimotor stage covers roughly birth to age 2. B) Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage; it is not tied to the formal operational stage, which comes after conservation. D) Concrete operational thinking allows reversible reasoning about real objects and is what passing the task reflects; hypothetical reasoning belongs to the formal operational stage.
questions.trap: Matching the child's age to the wrong stage label, or confusing centration with egocentrism.

questions.stem: Which statement is a limitation of using these data to describe how an individual child develops?

options.A: Only two tasks were used, so no clear developmental trend can be seen across the six ages that were tested.
options.B: The numbers of children differed across the ages, so percentages cannot be compared from one age group to another.
options.C: Each child was tested only once, which makes percentages an invalid summary of how children perform on the tasks.
options.D: Different children were tested at each age, so age differences may reflect cohort effects, not individual change.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) A cross-sectional design compares different children and cannot show within-child change; a longitudinal design would be needed. Why the others are wrong: A) Two tasks still show a clear trend, as the figure shows; the issue is the design, not the number of tasks. B) The groups were equal (30 each), so percentages are directly comparable. C) Testing once is not invalid; percentages of passing in each age group are appropriate summaries.
questions.trap: Citing a flaw that the data do not have, instead of the inability of a cross-sectional design to track individuals.

questions.stem: A teacher helps a 6-year-old succeed on the liquid task by guiding her to compare the width and height of the glasses, and the child then solves it. Which concept best describes the range of tasks the child can complete only with such guidance?

options.A: The sensitive period for language
options.B: The zone of proximal development
options.C: Assimilation of a new schema
options.D: Authoritative scaffolding of attachment

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with a more skilled helper. Why the others are wrong: A) A sensitive period describes a time when learning of a skill, such as language, is most efficient, not guided task performance. C) Assimilation fits new information into an existing schema, and the passage describes a task the child cannot yet complete alone. D) Attachment styles describe the bond between infant and caregiver, not guided cognitive performance.
questions.trap: Applying Piaget's terms (assimilation) to a social-guidance process described by Vygotsky.

passages.passage_text: A national health survey of 6,000 adults examined access to care by insurance and income. Respondents were grouped as uninsured, covered by public insurance, covered by private insurance with household income below the median, or covered by private insurance with household income above the median. Each respondent reported whether, in the past year, cost had caused them to delay needed medical care, and whether they had a routine checkup. Results are shown in Table 1. The survey was observational, and respondents were selected by a random sample of households. Uninsured respondents were younger on average and more often worked in jobs that did not offer coverage. Researchers noted that clinics in several low-income neighborhoods had long waits and few evening hours, and that interviews with clinicians indicated that some assumed patients who missed appointments simply did not value care. Interviews were conducted by telephone in English and Spanish with adults aged 25 to 64, and the response rate was 62%.
passages.table_data:
**Table 1. Access to care by group**

| Group | n | Delayed care due to cost | Routine checkup in past year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Uninsured | 800 | 42% | 38% |
| Public insurance | 1,200 | 22% | 61% |
| Private, below-median income | 1,600 | 15% | 66% |
| Private, above-median income | 2,400 | 6% | 78% |

questions.stem: Approximately what percent of all 6,000 respondents delayed care because of cost?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) Delayers: 336 + 264 + 240 + 144 = 984; 984 / 6,000 = 16.4%, or about 16%. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the rate for the largest group alone (above-median private), which is not the overall rate. C) This is the unweighted average of the four percentages ((42 + 22 + 15 + 6)/4 = 21.25), which ignores the different group sizes. D) This is the rate for the uninsured group alone.
questions.trap: Averaging group percentages without weighting by group size.

questions.stem: Why can the survey not show that lack of insurance causes lower checkup rates?

options.A: The sample was selected at random, which makes any comparison across the insurance groups impossible.
options.B: The checkup percentages were not reported separately for each group, so no comparison of the groups is possible.
options.C: Insured and uninsured respondents also differ in income, age, and job type, which could explain the gap.
options.D: Self-reported checkups are unrelated to actual health service use, which limits all survey research.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) An observational comparison has uncontrolled confounders such as income, age, and job type, so insurance status cannot be isolated as the cause. Why the others are wrong: A) Random sampling supports generalization to the population and does not prevent group comparisons. B) The table reports checkup rates separately for each group, so comparison is possible. D) Self-report can be inaccurate, but it is not unrelated to service use; it would not by itself explain the inability to infer causation.
questions.trap: Treating an association between insurance status and outcomes as proof that insurance is the cause.

questions.stem: The pattern in Table 1, in which access to care rises with insurance coverage and income, is best described as an example of:

options.A: a demographic transition, in which falling mortality and fertility shift the age structure of a population.
options.B: anomie, in which the weakening of social norms leads to deviance.
options.C: a self-fulfilling prophecy, in which expectations about a group produce the behavior expected.
options.D: a health disparity arising from social stratification, with unequal distribution of resources.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Unequal access to health care by social class reflects stratification, which affects health outcomes through resource differences. Why the others are wrong: A) The demographic transition describes shifts in birth and death rates, which are not shown here. B) Anomie (Durkheim) describes normlessness, not resource differences in access to care. C) The self-fulfilling prophecy concerns how expectations shape behavior; it fits the clinician example rather than the group differences in the table.
questions.trap: Choosing a theory term that matches a different detail from the passage instead of the pattern the question asks about.

questions.stem: The clinicians who assumed that patients who missed appointments simply did not value care are most clearly making which error?

options.A: The self-serving bias: crediting successes to internal causes and failures to external causes.
options.B: The fundamental attribution error: explaining behavior by disposition and overlooking situational barriers.
options.C: The actor-observer effect: attributing one's own behavior to dispositions and others' behavior to situations.
options.D: The just-world hypothesis: assuming that favorable outcomes are always deserved.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Clinicians ignored situational causes (cost, wait times, hours) and blamed patients' character, the fundamental attribution error. Why the others are wrong: A) Self-serving bias concerns how people explain their own successes and failures, not how they judge others. C) The actor-observer effect contrasts explanations for one's own behavior with those for others; here only judgments about other people are described, so it does not fit. D) Just-world beliefs concern deserved outcomes; the clinicians' explanation is about the cause of a specific behavior.
questions.trap: Choosing actor-observer effect, which contrasts self and other, when only judgments about others are described.

discrete.stem: After staring at a green square for 60 seconds, a person looks at a white wall and briefly sees a red square. This afterimage is best explained by:

options.A: trichromatic theory alone, because three cone types respond to short, medium, and long wavelengths.
options.B: opponent-process theory: fatigue of the green side of a red-green channel gives a red rebound.
options.C: dark adaptation, in which rods regenerate rhodopsin during prolonged time in low light.
options.D: feature detection by simple cells in the visual cortex, which respond to edges and orientations.

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Opponent cells signal red or green; after prolonged green stimulation, the fatigued green response yields a relative red signal against white. Why the others are wrong: A) Trichromatic theory explains color matching at the receptor but not complementary afterimages. C) Dark adaptation concerns sensitivity changes in low light, not colored afterimages. D) Feature detectors respond to edges and orientation, not afterimage color.
discrete.trap: Choosing trichromatic theory because it is the better-known color theory, even though it does not predict afterimages.

discrete.stem: Why can a person with thalamic damage still detect odors?

options.A: Olfactory receptor axons project directly to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
options.B: Odor detection occurs entirely within the nasal cavity without any involvement of the brain.
options.C: Olfactory bulb neurons project to cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay.
options.D: Taste receptors on the tongue take over the sensory function of detecting odor molecules.

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Smell is the only major sense whose primary pathway bypasses the thalamus on its way to cortex. Why the others are wrong: A) Olfactory axons synapse in the olfactory bulb and not in visual cortex. B) Perception of odor requires central processing. D) Taste provides a different modality and does not substitute for smell.
discrete.trap: Assuming all senses route through the thalamus before cortex.

discrete.stem: After seeing extensive news coverage of a plane crash, a person overestimates the likelihood of dying in a plane crash relative to driving. This reflects the:

options.A: representativeness heuristic, judging probability by similarity to a prototype.
options.B: confirmation bias, favoring information that supports prior beliefs.
options.C: availability heuristic, judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind.
options.D: functional fixedness, the inability to see novel uses of an object.

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Vivid, recent coverage makes plane crashes easy to recall, inflating their perceived probability. Why the others are wrong: A) The judgment is based on ease of recall rather than resemblance to a category. B) No prior belief or selective search is described. D) This concerns problem solving with objects.
discrete.trap: Picking representativeness because crashes seem 'typical' of danger, rather than recognizing recall ease.

discrete.stem: A patient with a left-hemisphere stroke speaks slowly with effort and in short phrases, but understands spoken instructions and recognizes her errors. The lesion most likely involves the:

options.A: left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area).
options.B: right hemisphere homologue of Broca's area.
options.C: left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area).
options.D: primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Nonfluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of Broca's aphasia. Why the others are wrong: A) Damage here causes fluent speech with poor comprehension. B) Right-sided lesions rarely produce this nonfluent aphasia in right-handed people. D) Visual cortex damage affects vision, not speech production.
discrete.trap: Mixing up Broca and Wernicke by remembering only that both involve language.

discrete.stem: A child who enjoys drawing is given prizes for drawing each day. When the prizes stop, the child draws much less than before the prizes began. This is best explained by:

options.A: extinction of a conditioned fear response once the expected prizes stopped arriving.
options.B: the overjustification effect: extrinsic rewards undermined intrinsic motivation.
options.C: drive reduction, as drawing satisfied a physiological need such as hunger or thirst.
options.D: a fixed-ratio schedule producing a pause in responding after each reinforcement.

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) The child came to attribute drawing to the reward rather than to interest, so removing the reward reduced the behavior below baseline. Why the others are wrong: A) No fear conditioning is involved. C) Drawing does not reduce a biological drive such as hunger. D) Drawing fell well below baseline instead of pausing briefly after each reward.
discrete.trap: Interpreting the drop as ordinary extinction rather than a decline below the pre-reward baseline.

discrete.stem: A sleeping participant shows low-amplitude, high-frequency EEG activity, rapid eye movements, and loss of skeletal muscle tone. The participant is most likely in:

options.A: stage N3 (slow-wave) sleep.
options.B: REM sleep.
options.C: stage N2 sleep.
options.D: stage N1 sleep.

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) This combination of a waking-like EEG, rapid eye movements, and muscle atonia defines REM sleep. Why the others are wrong: A) N3 shows high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves. C) N2 shows sleep spindles and K-complexes without rapid eye movements. D) N1 shows slow rolling eye movements and theta waves, with muscle tone retained.
discrete.trap: Choosing N3 because 'deep sleep' is associated with dreaming, when vivid dreaming is typical of REM.

discrete.stem: According to the dopamine hypothesis, antipsychotic drugs that block D2 receptors are most effective at reducing:

options.A: flat affect and social withdrawal.
options.B: hallucinations and delusions.
options.C: memory loss and slowed processing.
options.D: manic episodes and decreased need for sleep.

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Excess dopaminergic activity is linked to positive symptoms, which respond best to D2 antagonists. Why the others are wrong: A) These negative symptoms respond poorly to traditional antipsychotics. C) Cognitive deficits are less responsive to D2 blockade. D) These are features of bipolar disorder rather than the core symptoms of schizophrenia.
discrete.trap: Assuming antipsychotics treat all schizophrenia symptoms equally, including the negative symptoms.

discrete.stem: A cohesive committee, led by a strong chair, quickly agrees on a plan. Members privately have doubts but do not voice them and believe that everyone else agrees. The plan fails. This is an example of:

options.A: groupthink, in which pressure for consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation.
options.B: social loafing, in which individuals exert less effort in groups.
options.C: the bystander effect, in which individuals help less when others are present.
options.D: group polarization, in which a group's decision becomes more extreme than members' initial leanings.

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity within a cohesive group are hallmarks of groupthink. Why the others are wrong: B) The issue is suppressed dissent, not reduced effort. C) No emergency or helping behavior is described. D) Members' leanings were not described as moving toward an extreme.
discrete.trap: Selecting group polarization because the group's decision turned out poorly.

discrete.stem: Residents who agreed to sign a petition for a safer street were later much more willing to display a large 'Drive Carefully' sign in their yards than residents who were asked only about the large sign. This is the:

options.A: door-in-the-face technique.
options.B: low-ball technique.
options.C: peripheral route of persuasion.
options.D: foot-in-the-door technique.

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Agreement to a small request increases the likelihood of agreeing to a later larger request, consistent with self-perception and consistency. Why the others are wrong: A) This starts with a large request that will be refused and follows with a smaller one. B) This involves withdrawing an attractive feature after a commitment has been made. C) This describes how a message is processed, not a sequence of requests.
discrete.trap: Reversing the order of requests and picking door-in-the-face.

discrete.stem: According to Bandura, which experience typically produces the strongest increase in a student's self-efficacy for solving physics problems?

options.A: Successfully solving similar problems on her own
options.B: Hearing a lecture on the importance of physics
options.C: Watching a classmate solve a problem that she cannot
options.D: Feeling anxious while taking a quiz

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy. Why the others are wrong: B) Verbal persuasion is a weaker source of self-efficacy. C) Vicarious experience helps, but it is typically less powerful than personal success. D) High physiological arousal and anxiety usually reduce self-efficacy.
discrete.trap: Choosing encouragement or modeling over a person's own successful performance.

discrete.stem: In an experiment, participants are told they were randomly assigned by a coin flip to the 'blue' or 'green' group. They then give more money to members of their own group than to the other group. This best illustrates:

options.A: the fundamental attribution error, attributing others' actions to disposition.
options.B: in-group favoritism, which is predicted by social identity theory.
options.C: the just-world hypothesis, believing that people get what they deserve.
options.D: stereotype threat, in which fear of confirming a stereotype impairs performance.

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Even arbitrary group membership can lead people to favor the in-group to enhance their social identity. Why the others are wrong: A) The behavior is a bias in allocation, not an explanation of others' actions. C) The allocation was based on group membership. D) No performance was assessed.
discrete.trap: Believing that favoritism requires a history of conflict or real group differences.

discrete.stem: A student from a family that regularly attends museums and uses formal speech finds it easier to succeed in an elite university than a student without that background. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.A: Cultural capital, nonfinancial assets that confer social advantage.
options.B: Social capital, advantage derived from networks and relationships.
options.C: Anomie, a state of normlessness during periods of rapid social change.
options.D: Intragenerational mobility, a change in one person's status over her life.

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Familiarity with the dominant culture's tastes and styles functions as a resource that helps in education and elite settings. Why the others are wrong: B) The advantage described comes from knowledge and style, not from contacts. C) No normlessness is involved. D) The scenario compares students' backgrounds rather than one person's status over time.
discrete.trap: Confusing cultural capital (tastes, knowledge) with social capital (networks).

discrete.stem: In a period of sudden economic collapse, some researchers observe a rise in suicide rates as norms about aspirations break down. Durkheim would most likely attribute this to:

options.A: alienation from the products of one's labor.
options.B: rationalization of social life through bureaucracy.
options.C: symbolic interactionism, in which meaning is built through interaction.
options.D: anomie, a lack of social regulation and normative guidance.

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) In Durkheim's analysis, sudden change loosens social regulation, producing anomic suicide. Why the others are wrong: A) This is Marx's concept. B) This is Weber's concept. C) This is a theoretical perspective, not an account of suicide.
discrete.trap: Attributing the concept to Marx or Weber because all three wrote on social change.

discrete.stem: A city of 500,000 people has 12,000 immigrants and 8,000 emigrants in one year. Its net migration rate per 1,000 population is:
discrete.explanation: Correct: D) (12,000 - 8,000) / 500,000 = 0.008, or 8 per 1,000. Why the others are wrong: A) A decimal place slip would give 0.8. B) This is the net number of migrants in thousands, 4, not a rate per 1,000 population. C) This results from a different decimal error and has no basis in the figures.
discrete.trap: Giving the net count in thousands (4) or slipping a decimal place when converting to a rate per 1,000.

sources: Wikipedia Net migration rate; CIA World Factbook definition

discrete.stem: A researcher conducts 20 independent hypothesis tests at alpha = 0.05 in a situation in which none of the null hypotheses is false. About how many significant results are expected by chance?
discrete.explanation: Correct: C) 20 x 0.05 = 1 expected Type I error. Why the others are wrong: A) With alpha = 0.05, some false positives are expected even when no effect exists. B) This would correspond to alpha of 0.25. D) This would occur only if every test were significant, which is not expected.
discrete.trap: Assuming that no significant results can occur when the null hypotheses are all true.

sources: Duke RDAC Multiple Comparisons core guide; biostathandbook.com multiple comparisons
